Bronchiolitis

Bronchiolitis is inflammation of the small airways (Bronchioles) in infants and very young children < 2 years of age leading to fever, cough, rhinorrhea and wheezing, severe cases develop respiratory distress.

There is no agreed on diagnostic criteria for this illness, and it can be easily misdiagnosed as pneumonia or Asthma

It is mild and self limited in most cases

Annajurlina, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Etiology

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is responsible for more than 50% of cases of bronchiolitis. Other agents include human metapneumovirus, rhinovirus, parainfluenza, influenza, bocavirus, and adenovirus.

Viral bronchiolitis is rarely followed by bacterial superinfection.

NIAID, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Risk factors

Preterm infants

Low birth weight

Age < 5 months

Low socioeconomic status

Airway anomalies and chronic lung diseases

Immune deficiency disorders

Parental smoking

Pathophysiology

Infection causes inflammation of the small airways (bronchioles) leading to edema, small airway epithelial cell necrosis and sloughing, increased mucus production and mucus plugs, and bronchospasm, all of these factors increase resistance in the small airways

Annajurlina, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

So resistance in the small airways is increased during both inspiration and expiration, but because the radius of an airway is smaller during expiration, this result in wheezing, air trapping, and lung hyperinflation. If the airway is obstructed fully, trapped distal air will be resorbed and the child will develop atelectasis. Hypoxemia is a consequence of ventilation-perfusion mismatch. With severe obstructive disease, hypercapnia can develop.

Epidemiology

Over 100,000 young children are hospitalized annually in the United States with the diagnosis of bronchiolitis, making it the most common diagnosis resulting in hospitalization for children younger than 1 yr.

Bronchiolitis is more common in males, those exposed to second-hand tobacco smoke, those who have not been breastfed, and those living in crowded conditions. Risk is also higher for infants with mothers who smoked during pregnancy.

Older family members, including older siblings, are a common source of infection; they might experience only minor upper respiratory symptoms (colds) given that bronchiolar edema may be less clinically apparent as airway size increases.

Clinical features

The infant first develops signs of upper respiratory tract infection with sneezing and clear rhinorrhea and may be accompanied by decrease appetite and fever.

Gradually, respiratory distress occur, with paroxysmal cough, dyspnea, and irritability. The infant is often tachypneic, which can interfere with feeding.

respiratory distress manifest as increased Work of breathing, with nasal flaring and subcostal and intercostal retractions, increased respiratory rate

wheezing and crackles usually present and Expiratory time may be prolonged.

Complete obstruction to airflow can eliminate the turbulence that causes wheezing; thus the lack of audible wheezing is not reassuring if the infant shows other signs of respiratory distress.

So Poorly audible breath sounds suggest severe disease with nearly complete bronchiolar obstruction.

Apneic event may precede lower respiratory signs early in the disease, particularly with very young infants. Term infants at a postconceptual age of <44 weeks and preterm infants at postconceptual age <48 weeks are at highest risk for apneic events.

Dehydration can also occur due to poor feeding and tachypnea.

Hypoxemia, cyanosis, altered mental status, are signs of severe disease

Diagnosis

Diagnosis is clinical and does not require laboratory or radiologic studies:

Patients with bronchiolitis are <2 years old (peaking presentation is 6 to12 months of age)

Have an URI (cough and rhinorrhea), and wheezing

Do not have a past history or family history of wheezing or atopic disease

present during an RSV or other respiratory viral pathogen outbreak.

Chest x rays may show areas of atelectasis in bronchiolitis and may be difficult to distinguish from bacterial pneumonia; so it is quite confusing

And as a result, obtaining chest radiography in a patient whose clinical course and exam are consistent with bronchiolitis may encourage unnecessary antibiotic use.

Matteo Di Nardo, Daniela, Francesca Stoppa, Corrado Cecchetti, Marco Marano and NicolPerrottaa Pirozzi, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Laboratory testing is also not routinely indicated; the white blood cell and differential counts are usually normal and are not predictive of bacterial superinfection.

Viral testing (polymerase chain reaction, or rapid immunofluorescence) is not routinely recommended in the diagnosis of bronchiolitis but may be helpful if such testing prevents more invasive evaluations.

Concurrent serious bacterial infection (sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis) is unlikely and confirmation of viral bronchiolitis may prevent the need for a sepsis evaluation in the young febrile infant.

For young children with wheezing in whom the presentation does not clinically fit with the diagnosis of bronchiolitis, including those without other signs of viral infection, with very severe presentation, or complicated clinical course, further workup should be considered (radiology and laboratory tests)

Children with recurrent or refractory episodes of wheezing in infancy, particularly if associated with failure to thrive, may require evaluation for chronic disorders such as cystic fibrosis or immunodeficiency.

Otitis media is a common complication to bronchiolitis

Differential diagnosis

Asthma: Bronchiolitis and asthma both have wheezing as its most prominent clinical sign.

Most infants with bronchiolitis are unresponsive to both β-agonists and corticosteroids.

Pneumonia: pneumonia can have all the bronchiolitis symptoms but it comes with laboratory findings such as leukocytosis

Treatment

The treatment of children with viral bronchiolitis is supportive management.

Those who are experiencing respiratory distress (hypoxia, inability to feed, apnea, extreme tachypnea) should be hospitalized.

Risk factors for severe disease include younger age, preterm birth, or underlying comorbidity such as cardiovascular, pulmonary, neurologic, or immunologic disease.

Hypoxemic children (< 90%)should receive supplemental oxygen. Oxygen can be administered via nasal cannula or Hi-flow nasal cannula in moderate to severe cases or via positive pressure ventilation (CPAP) in severe cases.

Hydration should also be given to children with severe disease. Fluids can be administered intravenously or enterally via nasogastric tube, NG feeding preferred and it is indicated when respiratory rate > 60 breath/min to prevent aspiration

Frequent suctioning of nasal and oral secretions often provides relief of distress and improves work of breathing and ability to feed, although this should be limited to the nares or oropharynx because deep tracheal suctioning does not provide additional benefit.

Chest physiotherapy provides no benefit to children with bronchiolitis.

Albuterol and corticosteroids are proven ineffective in bronchiolitis; and neither are currently recommended for management.

Nebulized hypertonic saline decreases mucus production and is still used in bronchiolitis although most studies fail to demonstrate it being beneficial

Nasal vasoconstrictors are not indicated and have resulted in tachydysrhythmias.

Racemic epinephrine has not been found to improve length of stay or clinical outcomes among inpatients with bronchiolitis, but there is some evidence suggesting it reducing hospitalization rates if used outpatient.

Ribavirin, the only currently available antiviral medication targeting RSV, is also not currently recommended, because of minimal impact on disease outcomes, and because it is costly, difficulty to administer, and associated with multiple toxicities.

Prognosis

Infants with acute bronchiolitis are at highest risk for further respiratory compromise in the first 72 hours after onset of cough and dyspnea.

severity increases over the first 3 to 5 days with total duration of illness 7 to 14 days, So, in severe disease, disposition is done when the patient is well after the 5 day mark

Mortality rate is <1% in developed countries, with death attributable to respiratory arrest and/or failure or severe dehydration and electrolyte disturbances. A majority of deaths due to bronchiolitis occur in children with complex medical conditions or comorbidities such as bronchopulmonary dysplasia, congenital heart disease, or immunodeficiency.

Prevention

Meticulous hand hygiene while dealing with these children is the best measure to prevent transmission of the viruses responsible for bronchiolitis.

Palivizumab, an intramuscular monoclonal antibody to the RSV F protein, may be given as a prophylactic agent. Palivizumab has been demonstrated to reduce risk of hospitalization due to RSV bronchiolitis

Palivizumab indications:

In children born at <29 wk completed gestation

In children with significant heart disease or chronic lung disease of prematurity

And it is may be considered in infants with neuromuscular disease and immunocompromised states.
